why: "Prisoner" is the reading of nearly every manuscript, and it is the harder one: Paul opens no other letter this way. The other readings replace it with the titles of his other letters ("apostle," as in 2 Corinthians 1:1; "slave," as in Romans 1:1).

p: The oldest manuscripts call Apphia "our sister." The Byzantine text and the KJV call her "beloved."

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House, Westcott-Hort; Codex Sinaiticus (01, 300s), Alexandrinus (02, 400s), the first hand of Claromontanus (D 06, 400s or 500s), Augiensis (F 010), Boernerianus (G 012), 048, 33, 81, 1739, 1881; Old Latin, Vulgate, Coptic; Pelagius, Jerome
Byzantine text and Textus Receptus (KJV "beloved Apphia"); a corrector of Claromontanus, K, L, Ψ; Chrysostom, Theodore of Mopsuestia
629, some Old Latin copies, the Clementine Vulgate, the Harklean Syriac; Ambrosiaster (both words)

why: "Sister" has the older and wider support, in the Greek manuscripts and in the early translations. "Beloved" may have come in to match "Philemon, whom we love" (Greek agapētō) in 1:1, and the mixed reading simply combines the two.
b: Lightfoot weighed both directions: a copyist might have added "beloved" to match 1:1, or replaced it with "sister" out of a false delicacy about calling a woman "beloved." Theodore of Mopsuestia, who read "beloved," felt he had to explain that Paul meant nothing improper by it. Lightfoot chose "sister" because the ancient evidence is decidedly in its favor.

p: Some manuscripts use the same preposition (eis) for the Lord and the saints. The English hardly changes.

why: Paul elsewhere uses eis with faith far more often, so a copyist would easily change the rarer pros to match the eis of the next phrase. The change of preposition in most witnesses is the harder reading.
b: Lightfoot explained the change of prepositions: pros for the faith that reaches "towards" Christ, eis for the love that is put to work "upon" people, and he noted that "some good copies read eis here in both clauses." See the note on the crossed order of this verse.

a: every good thing that is ours
p: One Greek letter: hēmin, "us," or hymin, "you." The editions print "us"; the KJV reads "you."

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House, Westcott-Hort, Byzantine text; Alexandrinus (02), Ephraemi (C 04), Claromontanus (D 06), K, L, Ψ, 048; Ambrosiaster, Pelagius, Jerome, Theodore

readings.plain: every good thing that is yours

why: The witnesses are closely divided, and the two words sounded alike when read aloud. "Us" has strong support in both the early and the Byzantine witnesses, and copyists who thought the prayer was only about Philemon's household would be tempted to change "us" to "you" (Lightfoot's argument).
b: Lightfoot granted that "you" has slightly better support but preferred "us" as the more natural sense: every good thing believers have through the good news. With "you," the good things are those already at work in Philemon's household. The meaning of the prayer changes little.

p: Most editions read "I had much joy." The Byzantine text reads "we have much thanks"; the KJV "we have great joy."

Byzantine text (Robinson-Pierpont); Stephanus' Textus Receptus
The Textus Receptus as printed by Scrivener, the Greek behind the KJV ("For we have great joy")

why: The critical editions agree on "joy" and the singular "I had." The letter speaks in Paul's own voice from 1:4 on, and the plural "we have" looks like a change toward the plural of 1:1. "Thanks" (charin) and "joy" (charan) differ by one vowel.
b: Lightfoot judged "thanks" to be "absolutely condemned by the paucity of ancient authority," and noted that the Textus Receptus itself is divided: Stephanus printed it, but the Elzevir edition did not. That is why the KJV, which follows the Textus Receptus, still says "joy."

t: Is "receive him" in the Greek of 1:12?
p: The oldest text breaks off without a main verb. Most later copies add "you, then, receive him," as the KJV does.

readings.en: whom I sent back to you, him, that is, my own heart: receive him

why: The short text is the harder reading: its sentence has no main verb, and the command "welcome him" does not come until 1:17. Copyists finished the sentence by borrowing the verb of 1:17, and they did it in several different ways, which shows that the words were added.
b: Lightfoot agreed that the added words "give the right construction" but rejected them for lack of early support: Paul starts a sentence, breaks off into other clauses, and only picks up the main point in 1:17. The many forms of the addition in the manuscripts (with or without "to you," with "receive him" in different places) are listed in the apparatus.

p: The earliest papyrus of these verses has no "Amen." Sinaiticus, the Byzantine text and the KJV add it.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Westcott-Hort; Papyrus 87 (about 250), Alexandrinus (02), the first hand of Claromontanus (D 06), 048, 33, 81, 1881; some Coptic copies; Ambrosiaster, Jerome
Tyndale House edition, Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV); Sinaiticus (01), Ephraemi (C 04), a corrector of Claromontanus, K, L, P, Ψ; Old Latin, Vulgate, Syriac; Chrysostom, Theodore

why: Papyrus 87, a fragment dated about 250 that holds 1:13-15 and 1:24-25 (now at the University of Cologne), ends without "Amen," with Alexandrinus and others. The word was easily added at the end of a letter read in church.
b: After the blessing, many manuscripts add a note (a subscription) that is not part of the letter. Sinaiticus, Ephraemi and 33 have only "To Philemon." Codex K and the Textus Receptus have "To Philemon, written from Rome by Onesimus a household slave," which the KJV prints after the last verse. Later copies make Philemon and Apphia "the masters of Onesimus" and Archippus "the deacon of the church in Colossae," and one family adds that Onesimus was martyred in Rome. These notes show what later readers believed, not what Paul wrote.
